hints: Focus on what the word oxidation really means here, adding oxygen or removing electrons to turn a pollutant into a cleaner product.
Look at carbon monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons first, both still have carbon that can gain more oxygen to become carbon dioxide.
Now think about nitrogen dioxide, to make it harmless you need to strip oxygen away from nitrogen, so ask yourself if that is oxidation or the opposite process.
walkthrough:
**Recall what a catalytic converter does**

Great start, remember a modern converter does two jobs at once. It oxidises some pollutants and reduces others.

Oxidation = gain of oxygen. Reduction = loss of oxygen.

**Check oxidation of carbon monoxide**

Carbon monoxide is formed by incomplete combustion. It can still be oxidised further to carbon dioxide, which is much less toxic.

$$2\text{CO} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2$$

**Check oxidation of unburnt hydrocarbons**

Unburnt hydrocarbons are fuel molecules that escaped burning. They too can be oxidised completely to carbon dioxide and water.

$$\text{C}_x\text{H}_y + \left(x + \frac{y}{4}\right)\text{O}_2 \rightarrow x\text{CO}_2 + \frac{y}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Check nitrogen dioxide**

Nitrogen dioxide needs the opposite treatment. To remove it we strip oxygen off to give harmless nitrogen gas, so this is reduction, not oxidation.

$$2\text{NO}_2 \rightarrow \text{N}_2 + 2\text{O}_2$$

So only 1 and 3 are removed by oxidation.

options.A: Incorrect. While 1 and 3 are oxidised, 2 is not. Nitrogen dioxide is removed by reduction to nitrogen, so including all three mixes up the two different catalyst functions.
options.B: Incorrect. Unburnt hydrocarbons (1) are indeed oxidised, but nitrogen dioxide (2) is reduced, not oxidised. This choice also wrongly leaves out carbon monoxide, which is a classic oxidation reaction.
options.C: Correct. Unburnt hydrocarbons (1) are oxidised to CO2 and H2O, and carbon monoxide (3) is oxidised to CO2. Nitrogen dioxide (2) is removed by reduction, so it is not included.
options.D: Incorrect. Carbon monoxide (3) is correctly oxidised, but nitrogen dioxide (2) is removed by reduction. This choice also wrongly misses unburnt hydrocarbons, which are oxidised.
